question: Which statements about PEP 3119 ("Introducing Abstract Base Classes") are correct?
options: It proposes a way to overload isinstance() and issubclass().
It proposes a new module named abc which serves as an "ABC support framework", defining a metaclass for use with ABCs and a decorator that can be used to define abstract methods.
It proposes specific ABCs for containers and iterators, to be added to the collections module.
It proposes ABCs for numeric types, which were added to the collections module.
Much of the thinking behind the proposal was about clarifying philosophical issues such as "what makes a set", "what makes a mapping" and "what makes a sequence".
explanation: PEP 3119 proposes three things: overloading isinstance() and issubclass(); a new abc module (an "ABC support framework" providing a metaclass and an abstract-method decorator); and specific ABCs for containers and iterators added to the collections module. The Abstract also states that much of the thinking was about clarifying philosophical issues like "what makes a set", "what makes a mapping" and "what makes a sequence". Numeric ABCs were NOT part of this PEP — they are defined by the companion PEP 3141 (a type hierarchy for numbers), which the Abstract points to.

question: According to the Acknowledgements of PEP 3119, who wrote the Rationale section and most of the section on ABCs vs. Interfaces?
options: Talin
Guido van Rossum
Phillip Eby
Bill Janssen
explanation: The Acknowledgements state that Talin wrote the Rationale as well as most of the section on "ABCs vs. Interfaces", and that for that alone he deserves co-authorship. The rest of the PEP uses "I" referring to the first author, Guido van Rossum.

question: PEP 3119's Rationale divides the usage patterns for interacting with an object into two basic categories. Which statement about them is correct?
options: The two categories are "invocation" and "inspection": invocation means interacting with an object by invoking its methods (usually combined with polymorphism), while inspection means the ability for external code to examine the type or properties of an object and decide how to treat it based on that information.
The two categories are "invocation" and "inspection", and classical OOP theory prefers inspection over invocation.
The two categories are "inheritance" and "composition", with inspection being the preferred pattern in Python.
Invocation and inspection serve opposite ends: invocation supports uniform processing while inspection forbids customizing decisions per type.
explanation: The Rationale says the two basic usage patterns are "invocation" (interacting with an object by invoking its methods, usually combined with polymorphism, so the same method call may run different code depending on the object's type) and "inspection" (external code examining the type or properties of an object and making decisions based on that information). Both patterns serve the same general end: supporting the processing of diverse and potentially novel objects in a uniform way while allowing processing decisions to be customized for each type. In classical OOP theory, invocation is the preferred pattern and inspection is actively discouraged as a relic of procedural programming — but the PEP argues this view is too dogmatic and inflexible for a dynamic language like Python.

question: The Rationale of PEP 3119 gives the example of asking "is this object a mutable sequence container?" using inspection. Why are neither of the two obvious tests correct?
options: Looking for a base class of 'list' produces false positives, and looking for a method named '`__getitem__`' produces false negatives.
Looking for a base class of 'list' produces false negatives, and looking for a method named '`__getitem__`' produces false positives.
Both tests are correct but too slow to be practical.
Both tests return the same answer, so they are redundant.
explanation: The Rationale argues that in Python, where almost any aspect of an object can be reflected and directly accessed by external code, there are many ad hoc ways to test whether an object conforms to a protocol — but the obvious ones are wrong: checking for a base class of 'list' generates false negatives (a custom mutable sequence not derived from list would be missed), while checking for a method named '`__getitem__`' generates false positives (many non-sequence objects define `__getitem__`). This motivates the generally agreed-upon remedy of standardizing the tests and grouping them into a formal arrangement.

question: Which statements about the remedy proposed in the Rationale of PEP 3119 — Abstract Base Classes — are correct?
options: The remedy is to standardize the tests and group them into a formal arrangement, associating with each class a set of standard testable properties, either via the inheritance mechanism or some other means.
Each standardized test carries a set of promises: a promise about the general behavior of the class and a promise as to what other class methods will be available.

ABCs are simply Python classes added into an object's inheritance tree to signal certain features of that object to an external inspector; tests are done using isinstance(), and the presence of a particular ABC means that the test has passed.
The generalized abstract semantic definitions that accompany each ABC method are enforced by the interpreter.

The promises made by an ABC are in the nature of a friendly agreement: while the language does enforce some of the promises, it is up to the implementer of the concrete class to insure that the remaining ones are kept.
explanation: The Rationale proposes standardizing the ad hoc tests into a formal arrangement: each test carries promises about the general behavior of the class and about which other class methods will be available. ABCs are Python classes added to an object's inheritance tree to signal features to an external inspector, and the presence of a particular ABC (tested via isinstance()) means the test has passed. The ABCs define a minimal set of methods establishing the characteristic behavior of the type; their standard semantic definitions are described in the documentation but are "not enforced, but are strongly recommended" — so option 3 is wrong. Finally, the promises are a "friendly agreement": the language enforces some of them and the concrete-class implementer must insure the rest.

question: The "Overloading isinstance() and issubclass()" section of PEP 3119 discusses design dilemmas. Which statements describe them correctly?
options: The authors repeatedly faced the choice between standardizing more fine-grained ABCs or fewer coarse-grained ones; earlier versions of the PEP considered separate classes like Set, ComposableSet, MutableSet, HashableSet, MutableComposableSet and HashableComposableSet.

PEP 3141 originally proposed to patch `float.__bases__` so that float and int could be considered instances of a user-defined ABC, but there are good reasons to keep the built-in types immutable, for one because they are shared between all Python interpreters running in the same address space (as used by mod_python).
The Sequence ABC promises the append() method, so it is ideal for a generic function that needs any sequence with an append() method.
The MutableSequence ABC requires not only append() but also various other mutating methods, so neither ABC fits a generic function that only needs append().
The solution proposed is a metaclass for use with ABCs that allows adding an ABC as a "virtual base class" (not the same concept as in C++) to any class, including to another ABC.
explanation: The section describes the dilemma between fine-grained and coarse-grained ABCs (early versions considered Set, ComposableSet, MutableSet, HashableSet, MutableComposableSet, HashableComposableSet). Patching `float.__bases__` was rejected: built-in types should stay immutable, partly because they are shared between all interpreters in the same address space (mod_python). The append() example shows the reverse problem: the Sequence ABC does NOT promise append(), while MutableSequence requires not only append() but also various other mutating methods — so neither fits a generic function that only needs append() (option 2 is wrong). The solution is a metaclass allowing an ABC to be registered as a "virtual base class" of any class, including another ABC.

question:
PEP 3119 proposes registering ABCs as virtual base classes for built-in types so that conditions like the following hold:

```python
isinstance([], Sequence)
issubclass(list, Sequence)
issubclass(list, MutableSequence)
isinstance((), Sequence)
not issubclass(tuple, MutableSequence)
isinstance("", Sequence)
issubclass(bytearray, MutableSequence)
```

Which of the following evaluates to False under this proposal?
options: isinstance([], Sequence)
issubclass(tuple, MutableSequence)
isinstance("", Sequence)
issubclass(bytearray, MutableSequence)
explanation: The PEP shows that after Sequence and MutableSequence are registered as virtual base classes of built-in types such as basestring, tuple and list, all of the listed conditions are true except issubclass(tuple, MutableSequence), which is explicitly asserted as `not issubclass(tuple, MutableSequence)`: tuple is immutable, so it is a Sequence but not a MutableSequence. Meanwhile isinstance([], Sequence), isinstance("", Sequence) and issubclass(bytearray, MutableSequence) are all true.

question: How does PEP 3119 propose to overload the built-in functions isinstance() and issubclass()?
options: The call isinstance(x, C) first checks whether `C.__instancecheck__` exists and, if so, calls `C.__instancecheck__`(x) instead of its normal implementation; similarly, issubclass(D, C) first checks whether `C.__subclasscheck__` exists and, if so, calls `C.__subclasscheck__`(D).
isinstance() is overloaded via a global registry of types maintained by the abc module.
The magic names are `__isinstance__` and `__issubclass__`, defined on the class being tested.
issubclass(D, C) calls `D.__issubclass__`(C) whenever D defines it.
explanation: The primary mechanism is overloading the built-ins themselves: isinstance(x, C) first checks for `C.__instancecheck__` and calls it with x if present; issubclass(D, C) first checks for `C.__subclasscheck__` and calls it with D if present. The magic names are NOT `__isinstance__` and `__issubclass__` — the PEP explains this is because the reversal of the arguments could cause confusion, especially for the issubclass() overloader (the hook lives on the second argument, the potential base class).

options: True, because list appears in `AppendableSequence.__subclass__` and `__subclasscheck__` checks each class in the candidate's MRO against that set
False, because AppendableSequence inherits no methods from Sequence
True, because every list is automatically an instance of Sequence
False, because list is not a real subclass of AppendableSequence
explanation: In the prototype, `__subclasscheck__` computes candidates as `cls.__dict__`.get("`__subclass__`", set()) | {cls} and returns True if any class in sub.mro() is among the candidates. For isinstance([], AppendableSequence), `__instancecheck__` tests {type([]), [].`__class__`} = {list} via `__subclasscheck__`, and list is in `AppendableSequence.__subclass__`, so the result is True. The asserts that tuple is NOT an AppendableSequence (and () is not an instance) also pass, since tuple is not in its `__subclass__` set. This is a simplified illustration of the mechanism — the next section proposes the full-fledged abc module implementation.

question: Which statements about the abc module as described in PEP 3119 are correct?
options: It is a new standard library module, written in pure Python, that serves as an ABC support framework.
It defines a metaclass ABCMeta and the decorators @abstractmethod and @abstractproperty.

ABCMeta overrides `__instancecheck__` and `__subclasscheck__` and defines a register method that takes one argument, which must be a class; after B.register(C), issubclass(C, B) returns True by virtue of `B.__subclasscheck__`(C).
isinstance(x, B) is equivalent to issubclass(`x.__class__`, B) or issubclass(type(x), B), which matters because type(x) and `x.__class__` may not be the same object, e.g. when x is a proxy object.
register() may be called with any object, including instances, to make them pass isinstance() checks.
explanation: The abc module is written in pure Python and serves as the ABC support framework, defining the metaclass ABCMeta plus the @abstractmethod and @abstractproperty decorators. ABCMeta overrides `__instancecheck__` and `__subclasscheck__` and defines register(), which takes one argument that must be a class: after B.register(C), issubclass(C, B) returns True. The PEP also notes that isinstance(x, B) is equivalent to issubclass(`x.__class__`, B) or issubclass(type(x), B), and that type(x) and `x.__class__` can differ (e.g. proxy objects). Option 4 is wrong — register() requires a class, not an instance.

question:
Consider the PEP 3119 example:

```python
from abc import ABCMeta

class MyABC(metaclass=ABCMeta):
    pass

MyABC.register(tuple)

assert issubclass(tuple, MyABC)
assert isinstance((), MyABC)

class MyClass(MyABC):
    pass

assert issubclass(MyClass, MyABC)
assert isinstance(MyClass(), MyABC)
assert not issubclass(tuple, MyClass)
assert not isinstance((), MyClass)
```

Which statement about this code is correct?
options: The two asserts after MyABC.register(tuple) are equivalent to asserting `MyABC.__subclasscheck__`(tuple) and `MyABC.__instancecheck__`(()).
Because tuple is a virtual subclass of MyABC, it is also a subclass of MyClass.
MyClass() raises TypeError because MyABC has no concrete methods.
register() can only be used with classes that already derive from MyABC.
explanation: After MyABC.register(tuple), issubclass(tuple, MyABC) and isinstance((), MyABC) hold; the PEP notes these are equivalent to the direct calls `MyABC.__subclasscheck__`(tuple) and `MyABC.__instancecheck__`(()). You can also subclass MyABC directly (MyClass), which makes issubclass(MyClass, MyABC) and isinstance(MyClass(), MyABC) true. Registering tuple with MyABC does NOT make tuple a subclass of MyClass — the asserts `not issubclass(tuple, MyClass)` and `not isinstance((), MyClass)` pass. register() works on unrelated classes, not only on existing subclasses.

question: In the PEP 3119 abc-module example, after `MyClass.register(AnotherClass)` and `AnotherClass.register(basestring)`, the assert `isinstance(str, MyABC)` succeeds. Why?
options: Because the superclass-subclass relationships are traced as: MyABC -> MyClass (using regular subclassing), MyClass -> AnotherClass (using registration), AnotherClass -> basestring (using registration), and basestring -> str (using regular subclassing).
Because register() copies all of AnotherClass's methods into str.
Because isinstance() only checks the exact type, and str is registered directly with MyABC.
Because basestring is a regular subclass of str.
explanation: The assert isinstance(str, MyABC) requires tracing superclass-subclass relationships that mix regular inheritance and registration: MyABC -> MyClass (regular subclassing), MyClass -> AnotherClass (registration), AnotherClass -> basestring (registration), and basestring -> str (regular subclassing). This demonstrates that virtual subclass relationships compose with regular inheritance. Note that str is a subclass of basestring (the PEP predates Python 3, where str is the only string type) — option 3 reverses the direction.

options: A() raises TypeError, B() raises TypeError (foo is still abstract), and C() works because foo has been overridden.
A() works, B() works, and C() works because abstract methods are only checked at class-definition time.
A() raises TypeError, B() works because it is a subclass, and C() works.
All three raise TypeError.
explanation: A class containing at least one method declared with @abstractmethod that has not been overridden cannot be instantiated. A() raises TypeError (foo is abstract), and B(), which inherits foo without overriding it, also raises TypeError. Only C(), which overrides foo with a concrete implementation, can be instantiated. The PEP also notes that such abstract methods may be called from the overriding method in the subclass, using super or direct invocation.

question: Which statements about the restrictions and implementation of @abstractmethod (PEP 3119) are correct?
options: The @abstractmethod decorator should only be used inside a class body, and only for classes whose metaclass is (derived from) ABCMeta.
Dynamically adding abstract methods to a class, or attempting to modify the abstraction status of a method or class once it is created, is not supported.
@abstractmethod only affects subclasses derived using regular inheritance; "virtual subclasses" registered with the register() method are not affected.

The decorator sets the function attribute `__isabstractmethod__` to the value True, and `ABCMeta.__new__` computes `__abstractmethods__` by combining the sets of the base classes, adding names with a true `__isabstractmethod__` and removing names without it.
If the resulting `__abstractmethods__` set is non-empty, the class is considered abstract and attempts to instantiate it raise TypeError.
explanation: All five statements come from the PEP's Note and Implementation paragraphs: @abstractmethod is only for class bodies whose metaclass is (derived from) ABCMeta; dynamically adding abstract methods or modifying abstraction status is not supported; virtual subclasses (via register()) are unaffected by abstractness; the decorator sets `__isabstractmethod__` to True and `ABCMeta.__new__` computes `__abstractmethods__` by combining the base classes' sets, adding newly abstract names and removing overridden ones; and a non-empty `__abstractmethods__` makes instantiation raise TypeError. (The modern abc module docs add that update_abstractmethods() now supports such dynamic changes.)

question: Which statements about @abstractproperty as defined in PEP 3119 are correct?
options: It is a second decorator, defined in order to define abstract data attributes; its implementation is a subclass of the built-in property class that adds an `__isabstractmethod__` attribute (class abstractproperty(property): `__isabstractmethod__` = True).
It can be used in two ways: the decorator syntax for a read-only property, or the longer form for a read-write property, e.g. x = abstractproperty(getx, setx).
Similar to abstract methods, a subclass inheriting an abstract property (declared using either form) cannot be instantiated unless it overrides that abstract property with a concrete property.
abstractproperty is a plain function that must be called with at least two callable arguments.
An abstract property automatically provides a default implementation that returns None.
explanation: The PEP defines @abstractproperty as a subclass of the built-in property that adds `__isabstractmethod__` = True. It can be used either as a decorator (read-only) or in the longer form for a read-write property, e.g. x = abstractproperty(getx, setx). Similar to abstract methods, a subclass inheriting an abstract property cannot be instantiated unless it overrides that property with a concrete one. (In modern Python this decorator is deprecated — @property combined with @abstractmethod is used instead.)

question: Which statements about "ABCs for Containers and Iterators" in PEP 3119 are correct?
options: The collections module will define ABCs necessary and sufficient to work with sets, mappings, sequences, and some helper types such as iterators and dictionary views; all ABCs have ABCMeta as their metaclass.

The ABCs provide implementations of their abstract methods that are technically valid but fairly useless; for example, `__hash__` returns 0 and `__iter__` returns an empty iterator, and in general the abstract methods represent the behavior of an empty container of the indicated type.

Some ABCs provide concrete (non-abstract) methods and can be considered "mix-in" classes; for example, the Iterator class has an `__iter__` method returning itself, fulfilling an important invariant of iterators.
The ABCs override `__init__`, `__new__`, `__str__` and `__repr__` so that all containers share one standard constructor and string representation.
Defining a standard constructor signature would unnecessarily constrain custom container types, for example Patricia trees or gdbm files.
explanation: The collections module ABCs (all with ABCMeta as their metaclass) cover sets, mappings, sequences and helper types such as iterators and dictionary views. Their abstract implementations are "technically valid but fairly useless" — e.g. `__hash__` returns 0 and `__iter__` returns an empty iterator, representing the behavior of an empty container. Some ABCs, like Iterator (whose concrete `__iter__` returns self, an invariant Python 2 iterators had to reimplement per class), act as mix-in classes. Crucially, NO ABC overrides `__init__`, `__new__`, `__str__` or `__repr__`: a standard constructor would constrain custom containers (Patricia trees, gdbm files), and string representation is left to individual implementations — so option 3 is wrong.

question: Why does PEP 3119 define no ABCs for ordering operations (`__lt__`, `__le__`, `__ge__`, `__gt__`)?
options: Because defining them in a base class (abstract or not) runs into problems with the accepted type for the second operand: if both list and str derived from an Ordering ABC, [1, 2] < (1, 2) would be implied, but in Python 3000 such "mixed-mode comparisons" are explicitly forbidden and raise TypeError.
Because ordering methods cannot be implemented in Python.
Because the standard library already provides an Ordering ABC.
Because sets require a total order, which cannot be expressed with ABCs.
explanation: The PEP's Note explains there are no ABCs for ordering operations because defining them in a base class runs into problems with the accepted type of the second operand. If an Ordering class defined `__lt__`, then if both list and str derived from Ordering, [1, 2] < (1, 2) would have to be defined (presumably returning False) — but in Python 3 "mixed-mode comparisons" are explicitly forbidden and raise TypeError. The PEP notes this is a special case of a more general issue with operations that take another argument of the same type.

question: Which statements about the Hashable ABC ("One Trick Ponies" section of PEP 3119) are correct?
options: It is the base class for classes defining `__hash__`, and the `__hash__` method should return an integer; the abstract `__hash__` method always returns 0, which is a valid (albeit inefficient) implementation.
Invariant: if classes C1 and C2 both derive from Hashable, then o1 == o2 must imply hash(o1) == hash(o2) — two objects should never compare equal if they have different hash values.

Hashable objects, once created, should never change their value (as compared by ==) or their hash value; if a class cannot guarantee this for certain instances, `__hash__` for those instances should raise a TypeError exception.
Being an instance of Hashable implies that the object is immutable.
A tuple containing a list as a member is not immutable, and its `__hash__` method raises TypeError because it recursively tries to compute the hash of each member.
explanation: Hashable is the base class for classes defining `__hash__`, which should return an integer; the abstract implementation returns 0 (valid but inefficient). The invariant is that equal objects must have equal hashes, and hashable objects should never change value or hash once created — classes that cannot guarantee this for some instances should raise TypeError from `__hash__` for those instances. The Note stresses that being hashable does NOT imply immutability: a tuple containing a list is not immutable, and hashing it raises TypeError because hashing recurses into members (option 3 is wrong).

question: Which statement about the Iterable and Iterator ABCs in PEP 3119 is correct?
options: Iterator derives from Iterable; the abstract `__next__` method raises StopIteration, the concrete `__iter__` method returns self, and an Iterator is what the built-in function iter() returns, i.e. it supports the `__next__` method.
Iterable derives from Iterator, and its abstract `__iter__` returns a non-empty iterator.
The `__iter__` method should always return an instance of Iterable.
Iterable and Iterator are the same ABC under two names.
explanation: Iterable is the base class for classes defining `__iter__`, which should always return an instance of Iterator; its abstract `__iter__` returns an empty iterator. Iterator derives from Iterable and is the base class for classes defining `__next__`; its abstract `__next__` raises StopIteration and its concrete `__iter__` returns self. The PEP stresses the distinction: an Iterable can be iterated over (supports `__iter__`), while an Iterator is what iter() returns (supports `__next__`).

question: Which statements about the Sized and Container ABCs ("One Trick Ponies" section of PEP 3119) are correct?
options: Sized is the base class for classes defining `__len__`, which should return an Integer >= 0; the abstract `__len__` method returns 0.
If a class C derives from both Sized and Iterable, the invariant sum(1 for x in c) == len(c) should hold for any instance c of C.
Container is the base class for classes defining `__contains__`, which should return a bool; the abstract `__contains__` method returns False.
If a class C derives from both Container and Iterable, then (x in c for x in c) should be a generator yielding only True values for any instance c of C.
The abstract `__contains__` implementation returns True for every argument.
explanation: Sized covers classes defining `__len__` (which should return an Integer >= 0; the abstract version returns 0), and when combined with Iterable the invariant sum(1 for x in c) == len(c) should hold. Container covers classes defining `__contains__` (which should return a bool; the abstract version returns False), and when combined with Iterable, (x in c for x in c) should yield only True values. These "one trick pony" ABCs represent single methods like `__iter__` or `__len__`.

options: It has the advantage of not requiring explicit registration.
The semantics are hard to get exactly right given the confusing semantics of instance attributes vs. class attributes.
A class is an instance of its metaclass, which further complicates the check.
The check for `__bases__` is a precise implementation of the desired semantics.
The PEP's strawman is to do it, but arrange it in such a way that the registration API also works.
explanation: The PEP considers overriding `__instancecheck__`/`__subclasscheck__` to test for the presence of the applicable special method (e.g. hasattr(x, "`__len__`")). The advantage is that explicit registration is not required. However, the semantics are hard to get exactly right because of the confusing semantics of instance attributes vs. class attributes, and because a class is an instance of its metaclass; the `__bases__` check is only an approximation of the desired semantics (option 3 is wrong). The strawman: "Let's do it, but let's arrange it in such a way that the registration API also works." (The abstract `__hash__` inside the class named Sized is a typo in the PEP; the intended special method for Sized is `__len__`.)

question: How does PEP 3119 define the Set concept, and how do the built-in set types relate to the set ABCs?
options: A set is defined as a sized, iterable container for which certain invariants from mathematical set theory hold; the most fundamental operation is the membership test x in s, implemented by `s.__contains__`(x) and already defined by the Container ABC.
A set is any class that defines a `__contains__` method.
The built-in type set derives from Set, and frozenset derives from MutableSet and Hashable.
The built-in type set derives from Set, and frozenset derives from MutableSet.
explanation: The PEP defines a set as a sized, iterable container for which invariants from mathematical set theory hold. The most fundamental set operation is the membership test (x in s), implemented by `s.__contains__`(x) and already defined by the Container ABC. The built-in type set derives from MutableSet, while the built-in type frozenset derives from Set and Hashable (it is immutable and hashable).

question: Which statements about the Set ABC in PEP 3119 are correct?
options: Not every subclass of Sized, Iterable and Container is a set: sets have the additional invariant that each element occurs only once (as can be determined by iteration).

Set defines concrete implementations of the inequality operations as subset/superset tests; set inclusion implements only a partial ordering, e.g. {1, 2} and {1, 3} are not ordered (all three of <, == and > return False for these arguments).

Because Set derives from Sized, `__eq__` may take a shortcut and return False immediately when comparing two sets of unequal length, and `__le__` may return False when the first set has more members than the second.
Sets cannot be ordered relative to mappings or sequences, but they can be compared to those for equality (and then they always compare unequal).
The issubset and issuperset methods found on the set type in Python 2 are supported by the Set ABC, as they are mostly just aliases for `__le__` and `__ge__`.
explanation: Set is a subclass of Sized, Iterable and Container, but not every such subclass is a set — the additional invariant is that each element occurs only once. Set provides concrete implementations of the inequality operations as subset/superset tests; inclusion is a partial ordering, so {1, 2} and {1, 3} are not ordered. Since Set derives from Sized, `__eq__`/`__le__` can shortcut on length. Sets cannot be ordered relative to mappings or sequences but always compare unequal to them for equality. Option 4 is wrong: the Python 2 issubset/issuperset methods are NOT supported — the PEP notes they were mostly just aliases for `__le__`/`__ge__`.

question: Which statement about the Set ABC's operators and hashing support (PEP 3119) is correct?
options: Set defines concrete operators for union, intersection, symmetric and asymmetric difference — respectively `__or__`, `__and__`, `__xor__` and `__sub__` — which should return instances of Set; their default implementations call the overridable class method _from_iterable() with an iterable argument, whose default implementation returns a frozenset.
The operators `__or__`, `__and__`, `__xor__` and `__sub__` are abstract methods that raise NotImplementedError.
_from_iterable() must always return a set built from the iterable and may not be overridden.
Set defines a concrete method _hash that returns the identity-based hash of the object.
explanation: Set defines concrete operators for union, intersection, symmetric difference and asymmetric difference: `__or__`, `__and__`, `__xor__` and `__sub__`, which should return instances of Set. The default implementations call the overridable class method _from_iterable() with an iterable argument; _from_iterable's default implementation returns a frozenset, but it may be overridden to return another appropriate Set subclass. Set also defines a concrete method _hash that computes the hash value from the elements — hashable subclasses of Set can implement `__hash__` by calling _hash, or reimplement the same algorithm more efficiently while keeping the algorithm the same.

question: Which statements about the MutableSet ABC in PEP 3119 are correct?
options: .add(x) and .discard(x) are abstract methods returning a bool: add returns True if x was added and False if it was already there; discard returns True if the element was present and False if it wasn't. Both abstract implementations raise NotImplementedError.
.discard is modeled after Java.
.pop() is a concrete method that removes and returns an arbitrary item and raises KeyError if the set is empty; the default implementation removes the first item returned by the set's iterator.

.clear() is a concrete method whose default implementation repeatedly calls self.pop() until KeyError is caught; this is likely much slower than creating a new set, but in some cases object identity is important.
The in-place operators |=, &=, ^= and -= accept an arbitrary Iterable as the right operand, including &=.
explanation: MutableSet adds add() and discard() as abstract bool-returning methods (their abstract implementations raise NotImplementedError; discard is modeled after Java), plus concrete pop() (KeyError on an empty set; the default removes the first item returned by the set's iterator), toggle() and clear() (default: repeat pop() until KeyError is caught). It also supports the in-place operators |=, &=, ^= and -= as concrete methods whose right operand can be an arbitrary Iterable — EXCEPT &=, whose right operand must be a Container, so option 4 is wrong.

question: Which statements about the Mapping ABC in PEP 3119 are correct?
options: Mapping is a subclass of Container, Iterable and Sized; the keys of a mapping naturally form a set, and the (key, value) pairs (which must be tuples), also referred to as items, form a set.

`__getitem__`(key), `__len__`() and `__iter__`() are abstract: `__getitem__` returns the value corresponding to key or raises KeyError (the abstract implementation always raises KeyError), `__len__` returns the number of distinct keys, and `__iter__` returns each key in the key set exactly once.

get(key, default=None), `__contains__`(key), keys(), items() and values() are concrete methods; keys() and items() should return Sets (the default implementations return "views"), while values() returns a sized, iterable container that is NOT a set.
For any mapping m, len(m.values()) == len(m.keys()) == len(m.items()) == len(m), and iterating over the items, keys and values should return results in the same order.
The built-in type dict derives from Mapping.
explanation: Mapping is a subclass of Container, Iterable and Sized. Its keys and its items — (key, value) pairs which must be tuples — each form a set. `__getitem__`, `__len__` and `__iter__` are abstract (the abstract `__getitem__` always raises KeyError); get, `__contains__`, keys, items and values are concrete. keys() and items() should return Sets (default: views), while values() returns a sized, iterable container that is not a set. The invariants require len(m.values()) == len(m.keys()) == len(m.items()) == len(m) and identical iteration order across keys, values and items. The built-in dict derives from MutableMapping (a subclass of Mapping), not directly from Mapping, so option 4 is wrong.

question: Which statement about MutableMapping in PEP 3119 is correct?
options: It is a subclass of Mapping; `__setitem__` and `__delitem__` are abstract methods, while pop, popitem, clear and update are concrete methods; notably, setdefault is NOT included.
It is a subclass of Mapping, and all of its methods — including pop, popitem, clear, update and setdefault — are abstract.
It is a subclass of Mapping that adds only one abstract method, `__setitem__`.
It defines setdefault as its only concrete method.
explanation: MutableMapping is a subclass of Mapping that also implements some standard mutating methods. Its abstract methods are `__setitem__` and `__delitem__`; its concrete methods are pop, popitem, clear and update. The PEP explicitly notes that setdefault is NOT included, and lists "write out the specs for the methods" as an open issue. The built-in dict derives from MutableMapping.

question: Which statements about the Sequence/MutableSequence ABCs and the Strings section of PEP 3119 are correct?
options: The built-in list and bytes types derive from MutableSequence; the built-in tuple and str types derive from Sequence and Hashable.

Sequence is a subclass of Iterable, Sized and Container; its new abstract method `__getitem__` returns an element of the sequence when called with an integer (or raises IndexError) and returns another Sequence when called with a slice object.

Sequence's concrete `__iter__` iterates over the elements using `__getitem__` with integer arguments 0, 1, and so on, until IndexError is raised; the length should be equal to the number of values returned by the iterator.
MutableSequence's abstract mutating methods are `__setitem__`, `__delitem__` and insert; its concrete mutating methods are append, reverse, extend, pop and remove, and it also defines sort().

Regarding strings, byte strings (bytes) derive from MutableSequence and (Unicode) character strings (str) derive from Sequence and Hashable; the PEP leaves defining the base interfaces for these types as an open issue (PEP 358 should be co-opted for the bytes type).
explanation: list and bytes derive from MutableSequence; tuple and str derive from Sequence and Hashable. Sequence (a subclass of Iterable, Sized and Container) adds the abstract `__getitem__` with its int/slice signature, and its concrete `__iter__` walks `__getitem__`(0), `__getitem__`(1), ... until IndexError. MutableSequence's abstract mutating methods are `__setitem__`, `__delitem__` and insert; its concrete mutating methods are append, reverse, extend, pop and remove, plus the in-place operators += and *= — but it does NOT define sort(), which is only required to exist on genuine list instances (option 3 is wrong). The Strings section reiterates that bytes derive from MutableSequence and str from Sequence and Hashable, and leaves defining the base interfaces as an open issue, possibly co-opting PEP 358 for bytes.

question: According to "ABCs vs. Duck Typing" in PEP 3119, what is the relationship between ABCs and duck typing?
options: ABCs do not mean the end of duck typing: Python will not require a class to derive from an ABC when it defines a `__getitem__` method, the x[y] syntax will not require x to be an instance of an ABC, and any "file-like" object with a write method can still be assigned to sys.stdout.
Once ABCs are introduced, every class must derive from the appropriate ABC or isinstance() checks will fail.
ABCs replace duck typing entirely: hasattr(x, "`__len__`") checks will stop working.
ABCs are only allowed to be used with built-in types.
explanation: The PEP is explicit that ABCs do not mean the end of duck typing: no class is required to derive from an ABC (e.g. BasicMapping or Sequence) when defining `__getitem__`, the x[y] syntax does not require membership in an ABC, and any file-like object with a write method can still be assigned to sys.stdout. There will be "carrots" (default implementations, and an improved ability to distinguish mappings from sequences) but "no sticks" — if hasattr(x, "`__len__`") works for you, great. ABCs are intended to solve problems that have no good solution in Python 2, such as distinguishing between mappings and sequences.

question: What does PEP 3119 say about the compatibility of ABCs with Generic Functions (GFs)?
options: ABCs are compatible with GFs: GFs use the classes (types) of the arguments as the dispatch key, allowing derived classes to override base classes, and since ABCs are quite ordinary classes from Python's perspective, using an ABC in the default implementation for a GF (e.g. @prettyprint.register(Set)) is quite appropriate; the ABCs can be viewed as optional implementation base classes.
ABCs and GFs are mutually exclusive designs; a program must choose one or the other.
GFs cannot dispatch on ABCs because ABCs are not real classes.
GFs require that all user-defined mappings derive from BasicMapping.
explanation: The PEP argues ABCs are compatible with GFs. A GF implementation uses the classes (types) of the arguments as the dispatch key, allowing derived classes to override base classes; because ABCs are ordinary classes from Python's perspective, using an ABC in the default implementation of a GF is appropriate — e.g. @prettyprint.register(Set) for pretty-printing sets, with implementations for specific subclasses of Set added easily. The PEP also expects no problems for RuleDispatch (Phillip Eby's GF implementation in PEAK). Even GF proponents won't deny the usefulness of inheritance: the ABCs can be seen as optional implementation base classes, with no requirement that all user-defined mappings derive from BasicMapping.

question: What does PEP 3119 say about ABCs vs. Interfaces?
options: ABCs are not intrinsically incompatible with Interfaces, but there is considerable overlap; "Interfaces" in this context refers to proposals for additional metadata elements attached to a class which are not part of the regular class hierarchy but do allow for certain types of inheritance testing.
Interfaces are strictly better than ABCs, so the PEP abandons the ABC approach.
An interface is a class that must appear in the MRO of every implementing class.
Interface metadata cannot be modified by applications.
explanation: The PEP says ABCs are not intrinsically incompatible with Interfaces, but there is considerable overlap. "Interfaces" refers to proposals for additional metadata elements attached to a class which are not part of the regular class hierarchy but do allow certain types of inheritance testing. Such metadata would be designed, at least in some proposals, to be easily mutable by an application so application writers can override the normal classification of an object — and the drawback is that classes are shared state, so mutating them may lead to conflicts of intent. The need to override classification can be handled more cleanly with generic functions, e.g. a "category membership" generic function that returns False in the base implementation, with overrides returning True for classes of interest.

question: Which statement about the abc module and the ABC helper class (Python 3.14 documentation) is correct?
options: The abc module provides the infrastructure for defining abstract base classes as outlined in PEP 3119; it provides the metaclass ABCMeta and a helper class ABC whose metaclass is ABCMeta, so an abstract base class can be created by simply deriving from ABC (e.g. class MyABC(ABC)), avoiding sometimes confusing metaclass usage.
ABC is a plain class with no metaclass, so multiple inheritance involving ABC can never cause metaclass conflicts.
The ABC helper class was added in Python 3.2.
collections.abc provides concrete classes (like list and dict) that derive from the ABCs.
explanation: The abc module provides the infrastructure for defining ABCs, as outlined in PEP 3119 (see also PEP 3141 and the numbers module). It provides the metaclass ABCMeta and the helper class ABC, whose type is still ABCMeta — so inheriting from ABC requires the usual precautions regarding metaclass usage, as multiple inheritance may lead to metaclass conflicts (option 1 is wrong). ABC was added in version 3.4, not 3.2. The collections module has concrete classes that derive from ABCs, while the collections.abc submodule provides ABCs that can be used to test whether a class or instance provides a particular interface (e.g. hashable or mapping).

question: Which statements about abc.ABCMeta (Python 3.14 documentation) are correct?
options: It is the metaclass for defining Abstract Base Classes; an ABC can be subclassed directly, and then acts as a mix-in class.

You can register unrelated concrete classes (even built-in classes) and unrelated ABCs as "virtual subclasses" — these and their descendants will be considered subclasses of the registering ABC by the built-in issubclass() function.
A registered virtual subclass does not get the registering ABC in its MRO, and the method implementations defined by the registering ABC are not callable on it, not even via super().
Python's virtual base class concept is exactly the same as C++'s virtual base class.
Classes created with a metaclass of ABCMeta have a register() method.
explanation: ABCMeta is the metaclass for defining ABCs. An ABC can be subclassed directly and then acts as a mix-in class. register() adds unrelated concrete classes (even built-ins) and unrelated ABCs as "virtual subclasses": issubclass() will consider them subclasses, but the registering ABC will NOT show up in their MRO, and its method implementations are not callable — not even via super(). A documentation footnote reminds C++ programmers that Python's virtual base class concept is not the same as C++'s (option 3 is wrong).

question: Which statements about abc.ABCMeta.register() (Python 3.14 documentation) are correct?
options: register(subclass) registers subclass as a "virtual subclass" of the ABC; after MyABC.register(tuple), issubclass(tuple, MyABC) and isinstance((), MyABC) both return True.
Since Python 3.3, register() returns the registered subclass, to allow usage as a class decorator.
Since Python 3.4, calls to register() can be detected using the get_cache_token() function.
register() requires that the registered class already be a subclass of the ABC.
register() makes the ABC appear in the registered class's `__mro__`.
explanation: register(subclass) registers subclass as a virtual subclass of the ABC: after MyABC.register(tuple), issubclass(tuple, MyABC) and isinstance((), MyABC) hold. Changed in 3.3: it returns the registered subclass so it can be used as a class decorator. Changed in 3.4: get_cache_token() can be used to detect calls to register(). The registered class does not need to be a subclass (it is typically unrelated, even a built-in), and the ABC does NOT appear in the registered class's MRO.

question: Which statement about `abc.ABCMeta.__subclasshook__`() (Python 3.14 documentation) is correct?
options: It must be defined as a class method; it is called from the `__subclasscheck__`() method of the ABC to customize the behavior of issubclass() without the need to call register() on every class, and it should return True, False or NotImplemented: True means the subclass is considered a subclass of the ABC, False means it is not (even if it would normally be one), and NotImplemented means the subclass check is continued with the usual mechanism.
It must return a boolean; returning NotImplemented raises TypeError.
It is an instance method that is called on each instance of the ABC.
Returning False from `__subclasshook__` defers the check to the usual mechanism.
explanation: `__subclasshook__` must be defined as a class method (e.g. @classmethod def `__subclasshook__`(cls, C)). It is called from the `__subclasscheck__`() method of the ABC and lets you customize issubclass() behavior without calling register() on every class you want to consider a subclass. It should return True, False or NotImplemented: True → the subclass is considered a subclass; False → it is NOT considered a subclass, even if it would normally be one; NotImplemented → the subclass check continues with the usual mechanism.

options: The `__subclasshook__` class method says that any class that has an `__iter__` method in its `__dict__` (or in that of one of its base classes, accessed via the `__mro__` list) is considered a MyIterable too.
The abstract `__iter__` implementation (while False: yield None) can still be called from subclasses, and the get_iterator() method does not have to be overridden in non-abstract derived classes.

MyIterable.register(Foo) makes Foo a virtual subclass of MyIterable even though Foo does not define an `__iter__` method (it uses the old-style iterable protocol, defined in terms of `__len__` and `__getitem__`).
Registering Foo makes get_iterator available as a method of Foo.
When the check fails, `__subclasshook__` returns False.
explanation: MyIterable defines `__iter__` as an abstract method; the given implementation (while False: yield None) can still be called from subclasses, and get_iterator() is a concrete part of the ABC that need not be overridden in non-abstract derived classes. The `__subclasshook__` class method returns True whenever cls is MyIterable and some class in `C.__mro__` has "`__iter__`" in its `__dict__`, so any class defining `__iter__` counts as a MyIterable. register(Foo) makes Foo a virtual subclass even though it lacks `__iter__` (it uses the old-style protocol of `__len__` + `__getitem__`); however, this does NOT make get_iterator available as a method of Foo — hence it is provided separately. When the check fails, the hook returns NotImplemented (not False), so the usual mechanism takes over.

question: Which statements about abc.abstractmethod (Python 3.14 documentation) are correct?
options: Using this decorator requires that the class's metaclass is ABCMeta or is derived from it; a class with such a metaclass cannot be instantiated unless all of its abstract methods and properties are overridden.
The abstract methods can be called using any of the normal 'super' call mechanisms — unlike Java abstract methods, these abstract methods may have an implementation.
When @abstractmethod is combined with other method descriptors, it should be applied as the innermost decorator (e.g. @classmethod above @abstractmethod).

Dynamically adding abstract methods to a class, or attempting to modify the abstraction status of a method or class once it is created, is only supported using update_abstractmethods(); @abstractmethod only affects subclasses derived using regular inheritance, and virtual subclasses registered with register() are not affected.

To interoperate with the ABC machinery, a descriptor must identify itself as abstract using `__isabstractmethod__`, which should be True if any of the methods used to compose the descriptor are abstract; Python's built-in @property does the equivalent of checking its fget/fset/fdel.
explanation: All five statements come from the abstractmethod documentation: it requires an ABCMeta (or derived) metaclass and instantiation fails until all abstract methods and properties are overridden; abstract methods may have implementations callable via super() (unlike Java abstract methods — a useful end-point for super-calls in cooperative multiple-inheritance frameworks); when combined with other descriptors, @abstractmethod must be the innermost decorator; dynamic changes are only supported via update_abstractmethods() and virtual subclasses are not affected; and descriptors must set `__isabstractmethod__` True when any composing method is abstract (built-in @property does exactly this by checking its fget/fset/fdel).

question: Which statement about the legacy decorators abstractclassmethod, abstractstaticmethod and abstractproperty (Python 3.14 documentation) is correct?
options: abstractclassmethod and abstractstaticmethod were added in Python 3.2 and are subclasses of the built-in classmethod and staticmethod respectively; all three decorators were deprecated since Python 3.3 because @classmethod, @staticmethod and @property/@property.getter/@property.setter/@property.deleter can now be combined with @abstractmethod, making them redundant.
abstractproperty was added in Python 3.3 and is the recommended way to declare abstract properties.
abstractclassmethod is a plain function that must be used instead of @classmethod with @abstractmethod.
The legacy decorators raise DeprecationWarning and no longer work at all.
explanation: abstractclassmethod and abstractstaticmethod were added in Python 3.2 as subclasses of the built-in classmethod and staticmethod. All three legacy decorators — including abstractproperty, a subclass of property — were deprecated since Python 3.3: it is now possible to use @classmethod, @staticmethod, @property, @property.getter, @property.setter and @property.deleter with @abstractmethod, making them redundant. They still exist for backward compatibility but should not be used in new code.

question: Which statement about abc.get_cache_token() (Python 3.14 documentation) is correct?
options: It returns an opaque object (that supports equality testing) identifying the current version of the abstract base class cache for virtual subclasses; the token changes with every call to ABCMeta.register() on any ABC.
It returns an integer counting how many classes have been registered with each ABC.
It was added in Python 3.10.
Calling it invalidates the ABC cache, forcing all subclass checks to be recomputed.
explanation: get_cache_token() returns the current abstract base class cache token: an opaque object (that supports equality testing) identifying the current version of the ABC cache for virtual subclasses. The token changes with every call to ABCMeta.register() on any ABC, so comparing tokens is how you detect that cached subclass relationships may be stale. It was added in Python 3.4 — update_abstractmethods() is the function added in Python 3.10.

question: Which statement about abc.update_abstractmethods() (Python 3.14 documentation) is correct?
options: It recalculates an abstract class's abstraction status and should be called if a class's abstract methods have been implemented or changed after the class was created; it returns cls to allow usage as a class decorator, it is usually called from within a class decorator (e.g. one that adds abstract methods to a dataclass), and if cls is not an instance of ABCMeta it does nothing.
It raises TypeError if the class still has unimplemented abstract methods.
It automatically updates all subclasses of cls as well.
It was added in Python 3.4.
explanation: update_abstractmethods(cls) recalculates an abstract class's abstraction status and should be called if the class's abstract methods have been implemented or changed after creation (e.g. methods generated by a class decorator such as the standard library's @dataclass). It returns cls so it can be used as a class decorator, and the docs note it is "usually... called from within a class decorator". If cls is not an instance of ABCMeta it does nothing (no error raised). It assumes cls's superclasses are already updated and does NOT update any subclasses. It was added in Python 3.10.
